facts.statement: Pehuenchesuchus is an extinct genus of sebecosuchian mesoeucrocodylian named after the Mapuche name for its discovery region.
facts.quote: Pehuenchesuchus (meaning "Pehuenche crocodile", after the Mapuche name for the region in which it was found) is an extinct genus of sebecosuchian mesoeucrocodylian.

facts.statement: The genus was described in 2005 by Alan Turner and Jorge Calvo based on a nearly complete lower jaw bone.
facts.quote: Pehuenchesaurus was described in 2005 by Alan Turner and Jorge Calvo based on MAU-PV-CRS-440, a nearly complete dentary (the main tooth-bearing bone of the lower jaw).

facts.statement: The animal possessed a narrow, tall lower jaw and lacked the tooth serrations found in other sebecosuchians.
facts.quote: This animal had a narrow, tall lower jaw, and differed from all other sebecosuchians by lacking serrations on its teeth.

facts.statement: Its largest teeth were the first and fourth, with the first tooth pointing slightly forward.
facts.quote: The first and fourth teeth were the largest, and the first tooth pointed forward slightly.

facts.statement: The preserved lower jaw bone measures approximately 210 mm in length.
facts.quote: The preserved jaw bone is about 210 mm long.

facts.statement: Researchers classified the genus as the most basal (earliest branching) member of the sebecosuchians.
facts.quote: Turner and Calvo found their new genus to be the basalmost sebecosuchian.

facts.statement: The type species, P. enderi, was named in honor of the character Ender Wiggin from Orson Scott Card's books.
facts.quote: The type species is P. enderi, named for Ender Wiggin, a character in Orson Scott Card's works.

facts.statement: Fossils were found in the Upper Cretaceous Río Neuquén Formation near Rincón de los Sauces in Neuquén, Argentina.
facts.quote: It was discovered in rocks of the late Turonian-Coniacian-age Upper Cretaceous Río Neuquén Formation (Neuquén Group, near Rincón de los Sauces, Neuquén, Argentina.

facts.statement: The animal lived during the Santonian stage, between 85.7 and 83.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Santonian to Santonian (85.7 to 83.6 million years ago)
